title: Body Systems
seo_title: Year 8 Science: Body Systems Worksheets (Australian Curriculum)
standard_text: Describe the structure and function of a multicellular system, including how cells, tissues and organs work together, and how the digestive, respiratory and circulatory systems interact (summary of the Australian Curriculum v9.0 Science content description).
meta_desc: Free Year 8 science worksheets on body systems: cells, tissues, organs and systems, and how the digestive, respiratory and circulatory systems work together. 100 questions with answers.
key_sub: Digestion, breathing and circulation together deliver nutrients and oxygen to every cell.
body_html:
How to think about it

In multicellular organisms, cells form tissues, tissues form organs, and organs form systems.

  • Digestive system: breaks food into small molecules that are absorbed in the small intestine.
  • Respiratory system: the diaphragm and rib muscles move air in and out; oxygen diffuses into the blood in the alveoli.
  • Circulatory system: the heart pumps blood through arteries, capillaries and veins to every cell, carrying oxygen and nutrients.
Example

Order from smallest: organ, cell, system, tissue

cells make tissues

tissues make organs

Answer: cell, tissue, organ, system

Example

Where are nutrients absorbed into the blood?

the walls are thin with villi

Answer: the small intestine

Common mistakes

  • Thinking arteries always carry oxygen-rich blood (the pulmonary artery does not).
  • Thinking digestion happens only in the stomach.
  • Thinking the lungs pump air by themselves (the diaphragm and rib muscles do the work).

faq.q: How do the digestive and circulatory systems work together?
faq.a: The digestive system breaks food into small molecules. They are absorbed into the blood in the small intestine and the circulatory system carries them to all cells.
Oxygen diffuses from the air in the alveoli into the blood, and carbon dioxide diffuses from the blood into the alveoli to be breathed out.

faq.q: Why does your heart rate rise during exercise?
faq.a: Muscles need more oxygen and glucose for respiration, so the heart pumps faster and you breathe faster.

items.q: Mei writes in a health journal: “You eat lunch and later have energy to play.” Which two body systems work together most here?
items.e: The digestive system breaks food into nutrients, and the blood carries them to cells.

items.q: Lachlan reads about a body system that moves blood that carries oxygen and nutrients to every cell. Which system is it?
items.e: The circulatory system moves blood that carries oxygen and nutrients to every cell.

items.q: The nervous system is an example of which level of organisation?
items.e: Levels: cell → tissue → organ → organ system → organism.

items.q: A group of organs working together forms a(n) ____. What fills the blank?
items.e: Organs → organ system.

items.q: A lung is an example of which level of organisation?
items.e: Levels: cell → tissue → organ → organ system → organism.

items.q: Oliver is studying the lungs. Which organ system is this body part in?
items.e: The lungs is part of the respiratory system, which takes in oxygen and gets rid of carbon dioxide.

items.q: Priya reads about a body system that collects information and sends messages that control the body. Which system is it?
items.e: The nervous system collects information and sends messages that control the body.

items.q: Which list goes from smallest to largest?
c: organ, tissue, cell, organism, organ system
cell, tissue, organ, organ system, organism
cell, organ, tissue, organ system, organism
tissue, cell, organ, organism, organ system
items.e: Groups of cells form tissues, tissues form organs, organs form systems, and systems form the organism.

items.q: Zara is studying the nerves. Which organ system is this body part in?
items.e: The nerves is part of the nervous system, which collects information and sends messages that control the body.

items.q: Ethan asks: what is the main job of the digestive system?
c: It moves the body by pulling on bones.
It collects information and sends messages that control the body.
It moves blood that carries oxygen and nutrients to every cell.
It breaks food down into nutrients the body can use.
items.e: The digestive system breaks food down into nutrients the body can use.

items.q: Priya writes in a health journal: “You climb stairs quickly.” Which two body systems work together most here?
items.e: Leg muscles work hard and need more oxygen from the lungs.

items.q: Noah is studying the stomach. Which organ system is this body part in?
items.e: The stomach is part of the digestive system, which breaks food down into nutrients the body can use.

items.q: Isla is studying the kidneys. Which organ system is this body part in?
items.e: The kidneys is part of the excretory system, which removes wastes from the body.

items.q: Ruby writes in a health journal: “You catch a ball thrown to you.” Which two body systems work together most here?
items.e: The eyes and brain track the ball, and muscles move your hands.

items.q: Mia reads about a body system that takes in oxygen and gets rid of carbon dioxide. Which system is it?
items.e: The respiratory system takes in oxygen and gets rid of carbon dioxide.

items.q: Noah is studying the trachea (windpipe). Which organ system is this body part in?
items.e: The trachea (windpipe) is part of the respiratory system, which takes in oxygen and gets rid of carbon dioxide.

items.q: Aarav asks: what is the main job of the nervous system?
c: It supports the body and protects organs.
It moves blood that carries oxygen and nutrients to every cell.
It removes wastes from the body.
It collects information and sends messages that control the body.
items.e: The nervous system collects information and sends messages that control the body.

items.q: William is studying the skeletal muscles. Which organ system is this body part in?
items.e: The skeletal muscles is part of the muscular system, which moves the body by pulling on bones.

items.q: A group of tissues working together forms a(n) ____. What fills the blank?
items.e: Tissues → organ.

items.q: The circulatory system is an example of which level of organisation?
items.e: Levels: cell → tissue → organ → organ system → organism.

items.q: A lack of which nutrient causes weak bones and teeth?
items.e: A deficiency disease happens when the diet lacks a nutrient.

items.q: What does lipase break lipids (fats and oils) down into?
items.e: Big molecules are broken into small ones that can be absorbed.

items.q: What are villi?
c: tiny finger-like folds in the small intestine that increase its surface area
items.e: Faster absorption.

items.q: Which problem can be caused by too little vitamin D in the diet?
items.e: A deficiency disease happens when the diet lacks a nutrient.

items.q: Which problem can be caused by too little vitamin C in the diet?
items.e: A deficiency disease happens when the diet lacks a nutrient.

items.q: Which enzyme breaks down lipids (fats and oils)?
items.e: Amylase → starch, protease → proteins, lipase → lipids.

items.q:
PersonEnergy needed per day (kJ)
an office worker9500
a pregnant woman10 500
a 13-year-old who sits most of the day8000
a builder13 000
How much more energy does a builder need than a 13-year-old who sits most of the day?
What does protease break proteins down into?
items.e: Big molecules are broken into small ones that can be absorbed.

items.q: Why is fibre important even though it is not digested?
c: It is broken down by amylase.
It helps food move through the gut and prevents constipation.
items.e: Roughage.

items.q: What does the large intestine mainly absorb?
items.e: From the leftover waste.

items.q: Why must food be digested?
c: Large molecules must be broken down into small ones that can be absorbed into the blood.
items.e: Small enough to pass through the gut wall.

items.q: Which enzyme breaks down proteins?
items.e: Amylase → starch, protease → proteins, lipase → lipids.

items.q: Which problem can be caused by too little fibre in the diet?
items.e: A deficiency disease happens when the diet lacks a nutrient.

items.q: Which problem can be caused by too little calcium in the diet?
items.e: A deficiency disease happens when the diet lacks a nutrient.

items.q: Where are most digested nutrients absorbed into the blood?
items.e: Long, with villi.

items.q: Which food molecule does amylase break down?
items.e: Amylase → starch, protease → proteins, lipase → lipids.

items.q: What are the seven parts of a balanced diet?
c: carbohydrates, lipids, proteins, vitamins, minerals, fibre and water
items.e: Each has a job.

items.q:
PersonEnergy needed per day (kJ)
a pregnant woman10 500
a 13-year-old who plays a lot of sport11 000
a professional cyclist in a race20 000
a 13-year-old who sits most of the day8000
Who needs the most energy each day?
c: a 13-year-old who sits most of the day
a professional cyclist in a race
a 13-year-old who plays a lot of sport
items.e: More activity needs more energy.

items.q: A lack of which nutrient causes kwashiorkor (swollen belly, poor growth)?
items.e: A deficiency disease happens when the diet lacks a nutrient.

items.q: When you breathe out, what happens to the ribcage?
items.e: Breathing in: diaphragm and intercostals contract, ribs up and out, volume up, pressure down, air rushes in.

items.q: Why does air move into the lungs when you breathe in?
c: The lungs suck it in like a pump.
The chest volume increases, so the pressure falls below the air outside.
items.e: Air moves from high to low pressure.

items.q: Which part of the gas exchange system is described here? “Carries air from the throat to the bronchi and is held open by rings of cartilage.”
items.e: Each part has a job.

items.q: Alveoli have a huge total surface area. Why is this useful?
c: Lots of gas can be exchanged at once.
Gases only have a short distance to diffuse.
Dirt and germs are trapped before they reach the alveoli.
It stays open so air can always get through.
items.e: Structure fits function.

items.q: Which part of the gas exchange system is described here? “Tiny hairs on cells lining the airways that sweep mucus and dirt up and away from the lungs.”
items.e: Each part has a job.

items.q: When you breathe in, what happens to the volume of the chest?
items.e: Breathing in: diaphragm and intercostals contract, ribs up and out, volume up, pressure down, air rushes in.

items.q: Which part of the gas exchange system is described here? “A sheet of muscle under the lungs that contracts and flattens when we breathe in.”
items.e: Each part has a job.

items.q: On its way into the lungs, air passes through a bronchiole. Where does it go next?
items.e: Nose or mouth → trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli.

items.q: When you breathe out, what happens to the pressure inside the chest?
items.e: Breathing in: diaphragm and intercostals contract, ribs up and out, volume up, pressure down, air rushes in.

items.q: What is the job of the bronchioles?
c: Tiny hairs on cells lining the airways that sweep mucus and dirt up and away from the lungs.
A sheet of muscle under the lungs that contracts and flattens when we breathe in.
Small branching tubes that carry air to the alveoli.
Tiny air sacs where oxygen passes into the blood and carbon dioxide passes out.
items.e: Each part has a job.

items.q: What is the job of the alveoli?
c: Small branching tubes that carry air to the alveoli.
Carries air from the throat to the bronchi and is held open by rings of cartilage.
Two tubes that carry air from the trachea into each lung.
Tiny air sacs where oxygen passes into the blood and carbon dioxide passes out.
items.e: Each part has a job.

items.q: In the bell-jar model of the lungs, what does the rubber sheet represent?
items.e: Pull it down: the balloons inflate.

items.q: Where does air come from just before it reaches a bronchiole?
items.e: Nose or mouth → trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli.

items.q: When you breathe in, what happens to the ribcage?
items.e: Breathing in: diaphragm and intercostals contract, ribs up and out, volume up, pressure down, air rushes in.

items.q: What is one weakness of the bell-jar model?
c: The balloons are too small to see.
The glass jar cannot move like a real ribcage.
items.e: Models are not perfect.

items.q: Where does air come from just before it reaches an alveolus (air sac)?
items.e: Nose or mouth → trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli.

items.q: On its way into the lungs, air passes through the trachea (windpipe). Where does it go next?
items.e: Nose or mouth → trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli.

items.q: When you breathe in, what happens to the intercostal muscles?
items.e: Breathing in: diaphragm and intercostals contract, ribs up and out, volume up, pressure down, air rushes in.

items.q: Alveoli walls are only one cell thick. Why is this useful?
c: Gases dissolve before they diffuse through.
Gases only have a short distance to diffuse.
Dirt and germs are trapped before they reach the alveoli.
Lots of gas can be exchanged at once.
items.e: Structure fits function.

items.q: Airways are lined with mucus. Why is this useful?
c: Gases dissolve before they diffuse through.
Dirt and germs are trapped before they reach the alveoli.
Lots of gas can be exchanged at once.
Blood carries oxygen away quickly and brings carbon dioxide.
items.e: Structure fits function.

items.q: Which part of the circulatory system has this job: carrying oxygen from the lungs to the body?
items.e: Red blood cells: carrying oxygen from the lungs to the body.

items.q: What is the main job of veins?
c: carrying blood back to the heart
carrying nutrients, water and waste as a liquid
carrying oxygen from the lungs to the body
items.e: Veins: carrying blood back to the heart.

items.q: Blood arrives at the right side of the heart. Where has it just come from?
c: the left side of the heart
items.e: Body → right side of heart → lungs → left side of heart → body.

items.q: Which blood vessel carries blood back to the heart?
items.e: A vein carries blood back to the heart.

items.q: Why are root hair cells long and thin?
c: to give a large surface area for absorbing water and mineral salts
items.e: They have no chloroplasts.

items.q: What does an artery do?
c: It carries blood through the tissues, where substances are exchanged with the cells.
It carries blood back to the heart.
It carries blood away from the heart.
items.e: An artery carries blood away from the heart.

items.q: Blood arrives at the lungs. Where has it just come from?
c: the right side of the heart
the left side of the heart
items.e: Body → right side of heart → lungs → left side of heart → body.

items.q: What does a vein do?
c: It carries blood back to the heart.
It carries blood through the tissues, where substances are exchanged with the cells.
It carries blood away from the heart.
items.e: A vein carries blood back to the heart.

items.q: Which blood vessel has a thick, muscular, elastic wall to withstand high pressure?
items.e: An artery has a thick, muscular, elastic wall to withstand high pressure.

items.q: Which blood vessel carries blood through the tissues, where substances are exchanged with the cells?
items.e: A capillary carries blood through the tissues, where substances are exchanged with the cells.

items.q: Blood leaves the body's organs and muscles. Where does it go next?
c: the left side of the heart
the right side of the heart
items.e: Body → right side of heart → lungs → left side of heart → body.

items.q: Which part of the circulatory system has this job: helping blood clot to stop bleeding?
items.e: Platelets: helping blood clot to stop bleeding.

items.q: Blood leaves the right side of the heart. Where does it go next?
c: the left side of the heart
items.e: Body → right side of heart → lungs → left side of heart → body.

items.q: Which part of the circulatory system has this job: fighting germs that cause disease?
items.e: White blood cells: fighting germs that cause disease.

items.q: Which part of the circulatory system has this job: pumping blood around the body?
items.e: The heart: pumping blood around the body.

items.q: What is the main job of the heart?
c: carrying blood back to the heart
letting oxygen and nutrients pass into the cells
items.e: The heart: pumping blood around the body.

items.q: Why is a capillary wall only one cell thick?
c: so that substances can diffuse quickly between the blood and the cells
items.e: A short diffusion distance speeds up exchange.

items.q: Is blood in the left side of the heart rich in oxygen or low in oxygen?
c: it has no oxygen at all
items.e: Blood picks up oxygen in the lungs and gives it to the body's cells.

items.q: Is blood coming back from the body in the veins rich in oxygen or low in oxygen?
c: it has no oxygen at all
items.e: Blood picks up oxygen in the lungs and gives it to the body's cells.

items.q: Is blood in the arteries going to the leg muscles rich in oxygen or low in oxygen?
c: it has no oxygen at all
items.e: Blood picks up oxygen in the lungs and gives it to the body's cells.

items.q: Cooper writes in a health journal: “You drink lots of water and later go to the toilet.” Which two body systems work together most here?
items.e: The kidneys filter wastes and extra water out of the blood.

items.q: Ella says the small intestine is short because it is called 'small'. What is correct?
c: It is shorter than the large intestine.
It is long (about 6 m) but narrow.
It is the same as the stomach.
items.e: 'Small' refers to its width.

items.q: Who first described how blood circulates around the body in 1628?
items.e: An English doctor.

items.q: Noah writes in a health journal: “You lift a heavy backpack.” Which two body systems work together most here?
items.e: Muscles pull on bones to lift the bag.

items.q: How does a reliever inhaler help someone with asthma?
c: It relaxes the muscles around the airways so they widen.
It adds oxygen to the blood directly.
items.e: Widens the bronchioles.

items.q: What happens in the airways during an asthma attack?
c: The muscles around the bronchioles tighten and the lining swells, so less air gets through.
items.e: Inhalers relax the muscles.

items.q: Kai uses a model of the lungs with balloons and a rubber sheet. What does pulling the sheet down represent?
c: the diaphragm contracting so we breathe in
items.e: Lower pressure in the chest draws air in.

items.q: Lachlan reads about a body system that moves the body by pulling on bones. Which system is it?
items.e: The muscular system moves the body by pulling on bones.

items.q: How long does it take for the pulse to return to resting after exercise? How could you find out?
c: Measure the pulse every minute after stopping until it matches the resting rate.
items.e: Plan a fair investigation.

items.q: Ruby writes in a health journal: “You touch a hot pan and pull your hand back.” Which two body systems work together most here?
items.e: Nerves send a message to the brain, and muscles move the hand.

items.q: Tom asks: what is the main job of the circulatory system?
c: It moves the body by pulling on bones.
It collects information and sends messages that control the body.
It moves blood that carries oxygen and nutrients to every cell.
It breaks food down into nutrients the body can use.
items.e: The circulatory system moves blood that carries oxygen and nutrients to every cell.

items.q: Amelia writes in a health journal: “You run a race and breathe hard.” Which two body systems work together most here?
items.e: The lungs take in more oxygen, and the heart pumps faster to carry it to the muscles.

items.q: Ruby models digestion by squeezing bread in a stocking. What does the stocking represent?
items.e: Small, digested particles pass through the walls.

items.q: Why do regular swimmers often have a larger lung volume?
items.e: Training effect.

items.q: Why do scientists use models of body systems?
c: Real organs are hard to see working, so models show how they function.
items.e: Every model has limits.

items.q: Jack counts his breaths: 14 per minute at rest, 30 after skipping. Which systems are working together?
c: the digestive and skeletal systems only
items.e: More oxygen in, more carbon dioxide out.

items.q: Mia measures her pulse: 72 beats per minute at rest and 140 after running. Why does it rise?
c: Muscles need more oxygen and glucose, so the heart pumps faster.
items.e: The circulatory and respiratory systems work together.

items.q: How could you measure the volume of air you breathe out in one breath?
c: Measure your chest with a ruler only.
Breathe out through a tube into an upside-down bottle of water and see how much water is pushed out.
items.e: Displacement of water.

items.q: Why do fit people often have a lower resting pulse?
c: Their heart is stronger and pumps more blood with each beat.
items.e: Exercise strengthens the heart.

items.q: Why does a cut eventually stop bleeding?
items.e: Clotting forms a scab.
